E1382.summary: Desire directed to its object, above all to God for wisdom; it collects the mind and, joined with labour, brings revelation, and esoterically works within the operations themselves.
E1382.body:
Atwood treats prayer first in a broad sense: “every desire of the mind is in its kind a prayer and preparative for the acquirement of its object” [III.4 ¶22]. Directed especially to God for wisdom, it collects the mind and, joined with labour (cooperation), brings revelation; “prayer especially, which is its principle exercise, is profitable for great undertakings” [III.4 ¶22]. She then goes further: “But the esoteric ground brings us acquainted with prayer in a far deeper sense” [III.4 ¶22], where prayer works within the operations of the Art; she reports that Iamblicus distinguishes three classes of prayer leading to union and the Divine Fire.

Asserted identities: prayer = the great desire of knowing — “for if you burn with a great desire of knowing them, that is prayer” [III.4 ¶22]; and prayer as the Divine Key — “It likewise is the Divine Key which opens to men the penetralia of Wisdom” [III.4 ¶24]. In the method, prayer thus appears both as the disposing desire of the operator and, in the deeper sense, as an active part of the work (the exact mode of that working is not spelled out in these records).

E1383.summary: The Preacher, cited by Atwood for the veiled, pointed nature of wise writings and for the need of a companion in the work.
E1383.body: Atwood cites the preacher twice. First, to illustrate the pointed, veiled character of the writings of the wise: “The words of the wise are as goads” [III.4 ¶19]. Second (with the reference Eccels. 4:8,9), in support of her point that the work needs a companion, a medium and a bond, since one alone labours endlessly: “Behold, two are better than one, says the Preacher” [III.4 ¶30; III.4 n27]. In both she uses him approvingly as support for her own position.

E1384.summary: The earlier, preliminary part of the practice, handed down inconsistently; Atwood holds that knowing it is insufficient without the ultimate theory.
E1384.body: Atwood speaks of the preliminary practice as handed down inconsistently, and insists that mastery of it does not suffice without the ultimate theory: there are “many even with a perfect knowledge of the preliminary work, and having the true Matter in Hand also and means of purification” [IV.2 ¶4] who nevertheless fail.

E1385.summary: The preparatory stage of the work: for Flamel, preparing the prime agents, the hardest part; for Atwood, a stage exercising every faculty of the mind, sometimes lasting years.
E1385.body:
Nicholas Flamel, quoted by Atwood, makes the preparation of the first principles or prime agents the most difficult part of the work, after which the magistery is easy: “For knowing the preparations of the prime agents, and then literally following the directions in my book, I could not then miss the work if I would.” [I.1 ¶57].

In Atwood's own voice the Preparation is a stage in which no part of the concord may be left out: one must not “deny any faculty of the mind its due exercise in the Preparation” [III.4 ¶28]. She also notes its length: “Years have been employed by some in the Preparation” [IV.1 ¶17]. Whether her Preparation is the same as Flamel's preparation of the prime agents is not stated in these records See also Preparatory Practice and prime agents.

E1386.summary: A practice Atwood defers to a later discussion, there to show the value of assistance; Norton describes it.
E1386.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) postpones discussion of the Preparatory Practice to a later point, where the value of assistance will be clearer: “when we come to speak of the Preparatory Practice which Norton, naively, and without much envy, describes” [III.4 ¶36].

E1387.summary: In an adept's account, the spirit that dissolves and cleanses the body of Light and draws from it a second, tinging Spirit.
E1387.body: Voice: an adept quoted by Atwood. The Preparing Spirit dissolves and purifies the body of Light and extracts from it a Second, tinging Spirit: “The Preparing Spirit dissolves the body of Light, and cleanses it from the corrupting causes” [IV.1 ¶10].

E1388.summary: Zoroaster's term, which Atwood reads as the Fire Spirit of Life, the supernatural centre of every living thing, which the Art sought to multiply and exalt.
E1388.body:
An adept quoted by Atwood pairs the Prester with the Sun: “the miraculous conspiracy that is between the Prester and the Sun, the external and internal fire of life, the thing desiring and the thing desired” [II.3 ¶41].

Atwood herself identifies it: “the Prester of Zoroaster which in the Chaldean sense means the Fire Spirit of Life” [II.3 ¶54] — the identity sustaining all things, the supernatural centre of every living thing. The perfection of the Art was “to multiply the Prester and place him in the most supreme Ether” [II.3 ¶56].

In a Chaldaic oracle she quotes, the Prester is the Flower of glowing Fire drawn from the matter springing from “The Matrix containing all things” [IV.2 ¶28]: “Whence is extracted a Prester the Flower of glowing Fire,” [IV.2 ¶28], flashing into the cavities of the world. The oracle passage is not further explained there.

E1389.summary: In Chaldaic oracle language used by Atwood, the powers of intellectual fire to which all things are subject and which follow their First Cause in order.
E1389.body: The phrase comes from the Chaldaic Oracle, taken up in Atwood's own discussion (the records do not separate the two voices sharply): “to these Intellectual Presters of Intellectual Fire all things are subservient by the persuasive will of the Father” [II.4 ¶33]; and “the Presters of Intellectual Fire follow in radiant order the will of their First Cause” [II.4 ¶38]. See Prester.

E1390.summary: In Flamel's account, the initial agents of the work, whose preparation must be known before the work can succeed.
E1390.body: Voice: Nicholas Flamel, quoted by Atwood. The preparation of the prime agents is the key requirement: “knowing the preparations of the prime agents” [I.1 ¶57]. In the same account Flamel apparently uses the phrase in place of first principles, though the identity is not explicitly asserted. See Preparation.

E1391.summary: For some modern Kabalists cited by Atwood, the pure attracting vacuum or understanding, born of the concentrated Divinity, that draws the central efficient into will and operation.
E1391.body: Voice: some modern Kabalists, reported by Atwood. The primitive Ether is born of the concentrated Divinity like a shower from a cloud, and is identified as “the primitive Ether, which is the pure attracting vacuum, or understanding” [III.2 ¶13], which draws the central efficient to will and operation.

E1392.summary: An author cited from the Epilogue to the Invest. Of Perfection, whom Atwood uses to show that the student must gather the dispersed teaching and test it.
E1392.body: Atwood quotes the prince (work given as Epilogue to the Invest. Of Perfection) in support of her view that the student must collect the dispersed teaching and test it by experiment: “let the sapient artificer, concludes the prince, studiously peruse our books, collecting our dispersed intention” [III.4 ¶20; III.4 n15].

E1393.summary: In Reuchlin, the second of the two catholic natures in the mirific Word: incorruptible, immutable and always subsistent.
E1393.body: Voice: Reuchlin, quoted by Atwood. Of the two catholic natures in the mirific Word, the second is set against the visible, changing nature: “the other nature or principiating substance is incorruptible, immutable, and always subsistent” [III.2 ¶24].

E1394.summary: The beginning or principle of the work, which Atwood identifies with the intention; hard to find because the rational ferment lies hidden in our life.
E1394.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood identifies the principium with the intention: “The difficulty is to find this principium, the intention” [APP ¶35]. The difficulty arises because the rational ferment is hidden in our life.

E1395.summary: The one source to which all things, thoughts and actions are resolved and from which every particular can be recomposed; the final term of the soul's ascent.
E1395.body: Atwood presents the Principle as the end of the soul's ascent — the ascent rises “afterwards to the Principle of things” [III.3 ¶26] — and as the one source into which all things, thoughts, passions and actions are resolved. Whoever reaches it gains more than possession: “he will not alone have that Principle, and be able to compose and renumerate every former particular out of the same” [III.3 ¶39]. The method apparently involves resolving everything into its source and recomposing from it. See also Principle of things.

E1396.summary: For the Hebrew Kabalists, a principle remaining in the life of fallen individuals that will in time restore them to their source in higher perfection.
E1396.body: Voice: the Hebrew Kabalists / Rabbis, as Atwood reports them. Even after the fall, “the principle of reunion nevertheless abides in the generated life of individuals” [II.1 ¶41], and in time it will restore them to their source in a higher perfection.

E1397.summary: That with which the intellectual energy of the intelligible world keeps perpetual, tranquil contact, and from that contact generates Light.
E1397.body: Atwood writes that the intellectual energy of the intelligible world “generates Light through a perpetual tranquil and quiet contact with the Principle of things” [II.4 ¶16]. See Principle, where the same phrase names the final term of the soul's ascent [III.3 ¶26].

E1398.summary: A real and efficacious principle that Atwood holds lies latent in human life and can be known only under specified conditions.
E1398.body: Atwood asserts “a Principle of Universal Science latent in human life, real and efficacious” [II.1 ¶39], which can be known only under specified conditions.

E1399.summary: What the Hermetic names Sulphur, Salt, Mercury and the elements refer to, as opposed to qualities; in Eudoxus, the principles of 'our Mercury' separated in the Third Key.
E1399.body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood states that the Hermetic names — Sulphur, Salt, Mercury, water, air, fire — refer to principles, not qualities, though “in the spirit they become qualities” [APP ¶81].

Eudoxus, quoted by Atwood, speaks of the principles of 'our Mercury' (Salt, Sulphur, Mercury), extracted after sublimation and then separated and purified in the Third Key: “the separation and the purification of the Principles of our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶7].

E1400.summary: In Boehme, the three leaves of the inner book (the image of God) in which he finds all that scripture teaches.
E1400.body: Voice: Boehme, quoted by Atwood. The inner book he opened, the image of God, holds everything scripture teaches: “my book hath only three leaves, the same are the Principles of Eternity” [III.2 ¶16].

E1401.summary: Inquiry from the inner, causal ground: for Atwood the true method for first truths, which then proves itself a posteriori by its effects.
E1401.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood sets the a priori method, inquiry from the inner causal ground, against the inductive method: “The a priori method is the true one for the discovery of the first truths” [APP ¶120]. Only the soul's lapse into selfhood hinders it. Once established, “it proceeds to prove itself a posteriori by efficient procedure, as it were by what is commonly called miracle” [APP ¶120]. See a priori ground.

E1402.summary: The ancients' philosophical method, contrasted with modern inductive science; long neglected, it is the ground Atwood wants philosophy to return to.
E1402.body: Atwood contrasts the ancients' method with modern inductive science and wants philosophy to “return with her instruments to work as formerly on the a priori ground” [III.1 ¶8], a ground long left uncultivated. See a priori.

E1403.summary: Author of works on Plato whom Atwood cites often on the Mysteries, initiation, the soul's purification and its union with the One, almost always in support.
E1403.body:
Atwood names Proclus among the Alexandrian revival figures who professed Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge, to be quoted later [I.1 ¶27]. She also lists him among the Neoplatonists whose surviving writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification [II.2 ¶9], and in the 'golden chain of Hermetic philosophers' who traced the poets' allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil [III.1 ¶25].

She uses him throughout in support of her own account:
- The mundane or phantastic spirit: “it folds itself about the indivisibility of true intellect (which is in its center)” [II.2 ¶15].
- Why Theseus and Pirithous were detained in Hades, a reading she endorses [II.3 ¶13].
- Deceptive images come before illumination: “In the most holy Mysteries, says he, before the presence of the god, the impulsive forms of certain terrestrial demons appear” [II.3 ¶22; II.3 n17]. She applies the same to the speculation of Wholes. In the Hymn to the Sun, demons keep souls in the body, forgetful of their origin: “Demons who machinate a thousand ills,” [II.3 ¶24; II.3 ¶25].
- Astonishment at the mystic spectacles: “Beauty shining forth astonishes those that behold it, converts the soul to itself” [II.3 ¶50; II.3 n53].
- Hercules' purification, the Elysian fountains and the Meadow as the prolific power of life: “the plain of Truth, he says, is intellectually expanded to intelligible Light” [II.4 ¶3; II.4 ¶16; II.4 n8].
- Grades of initiation and the soul's inward conversion: “there are indeed many steps of ascent, but all of them extend to the Paternal port and the Paternal Initiation” [II.4 ¶23; II.4 ¶29; II.4 n15, n21, n22]. Initiation comes through faith-given silence: “what else than faith is the cause of this ineffable muesis?” [II.4 ¶40; II.4 n29]. The goal: “This, then, is the Paternal Port and the discovery of the Father, according to Proclus, viz., an undefiled union with him” [II.4 ¶41].
- The twofold Apollonical Intellect, paralleling Wisdom and Power: “the prophetic power unfolds the simplicity of truth and takes away the variety of that which is false” [III.1 ¶45; III.1 n50].
- “Heaven, he says, is the intellectual contact with the intelligible” [III.2 ¶36; III.2 n31].
- To discover the One Principle one must be assimilated to it: “he must raise himself to that which is most united in nature, and to its flower” [III.2 ¶50].
- The god torn, preserved and renewed (Hymn to Minerva): “The heart of Bacchus, swiftly slaughtered king, Was saved in Aether” [III.3 ¶70; III.3 n47].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says he develops the ontological basis of the Iliad [APP ¶157]. She also praises his Commentary on the Timaeus, which treats Time as the image's participation of the Paradigm, against the relational view held by her addressee and by modern metaphysicians [APP ¶172].

E1404.summary: One of the alchemists' three periods, which Atwood identifies with the subjective life, the water below.
E1404.body: Atwood names the Profundity as one of the alchemists' three periods and explains it: “the Profundity is the subjective life, the water that is below” [III.3 ¶72].

E1405.summary: The final operation: casting the Stone, powder or medicine onto a metal or mercury to tinge or transmute it, which Atwood also extends to 'the imperfect metal of any life'.
E1405.body:
Projection is the application of the finished Stone, powder or medicine to a substance to transmute it. In Atwood's historical accounts: Arnold's “wonderful projections he made with the transmuting powder” [I.1 ¶43]; “In Dee’s diary we have the account of Kelly making projection with one small grain” [I.1 ¶66]; “However, I made projection of a part” [I.1 ¶73]. Flamel, after the magistery: “Having attained this, I came now to the Projection; and the first time I made projection, was upon mercury” [I.1 ¶57], turning it to silver, and with the Red Stone to gold. Van Helmont: “I have made projections divers times” [I.1 ¶76], casting a little powder on boiling quicksilver.

Technical conditions: an adept says the medicine must first be fermented with pure gold, or “there would ensue loss and damage in the projection” [I.3 n70]. The Hunting of the Greene Lyon says continually fermented medicine grows stronger: “And sure far it will be exalted at the last, And in Projeccion ren full fast:” [III.1 ¶65]. Atwood advises that “it is always best to make projection by degrees until the Stone yields no more tincture” [IV.3 ¶20], onto purified metal. She gives an alternative name: “the final Projection, as the metalline perfectibility of the matter is sometimes called” [IV.3 ¶19].

Some sources limit its importance. The fraternity of the Rosy Cross: “The fifth and last gate is projection.” [III.3 ¶63], which serves only for metals. Eudoxus deliberately leaves “the Projection of the Medicine” [IV.3 ¶16] undescribed, since success does not depend on it.

Atwood also applies the term beyond metals: the Mercury “projected on the imperfect metal of any life, dissolves, drawing away the foundation into itself” [III.3 ¶32].

E1406.summary: Mythic figures Atwood uses to picture the method of ascent as the artistic fabrication of the Fire.
E1406.body: Atwood illustrates the method of ascent as the artistic fabrication of the Fire, which Prometheus received from Vulcan and Minerva disseminated [IV.4 ¶8].

E1407.summary: Atwood's image for the goal beyond the sea of sense, which a haven and signal marks direct one to.
E1407.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) writes that beyond the sea of sense “there is a haven and signal marks to direct where the Promised Land is to be found” [IV.4 ¶32].

E1408.summary: Prophecies of the Fourth Monarchy that Atwood notes but does not dwell on.
E1408.body: Atwood reports prophecies foretelling the Fourth Monarchy — “Many prophecies there are of times to come” [IV.3 ¶49] — but does not tarry on them.

E1409.summary: A prophetic voice cited from the Book of Enoch on those who misuse secrets, and in the Ordinal on the feeding of the matter.
E1409.body: Atwood cites the prophet (Book of Enoch, cap. 64, sect. 2) in support: those who discover secrets and turn them to ill account are judged — “They have discovered secrets, and these are they who are to be judged” [III.4 ¶6; III.4 n3]. She identifies them with Geber's avaricious. In the Ordinal, as quoted, the prophet's words are cited as a wondrous mention of the feeding of the matter, 'If ye apply it to this intention': “Visitasti terram et inebriasti eam,” [IV.1 ¶12] (ours: 'Thou hast visited the earth and watered it').

E1410.summary: In Atwood's reading, the intellect's congenial life: our lapsed soul, hidden in her dark hypostasis.
E1410.body: Atwood glosses Proserpine as the intellect's “own congenial life, which is Proserpine, and that lapsed soul of ours, seated in her dark hypostasis unknown” [II.3 ¶11].

E1411.summary: A verse piece, apparently spoken by the Stone, cited by Atwood for the balanced state in which the principles neither die nor live during the severation.
E1411.body: Atwood cites the Prosopopoeia of the Stone (references given as Theatr. Chem., Tome 3, p. 764; Processus Chiica, Carmen Elegans; Vaughan’s magia Adamica) to illustrate the balanced state in which the principles neither die nor live during the severation: “I am not dead although my spirit’s gone,” [III.1 ¶53; III.1 ¶54; III.1 n59].
